articles.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
articles.description: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed. This sequesters a region needed by two effectors, the kinase CK2 and the ubiquitin ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which act sequentially to signal TDO2 degradation. The findings are now published in Molecular Cell.

articles.title: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?
articles.description: Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth. “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.” Why Phobos Is Such a Strange Moon Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites. Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth. More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA. MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home. If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth. “It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix. How MMX Will Orbit Phobos Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars. “If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX. From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi. Martian Maneuvers The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface. During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface. Idefix Rover: The First Penguin Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029. It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space. Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict. “It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead. Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France. The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.” The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says. Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says. Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.” What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters. How MMX Will Land and Collect Samples Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase. The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved. The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.” Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it. The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says. One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes. That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample. During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off. Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth. Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners. “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system. “MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

articles.title: Growing up together, apart
articles.description: There's something a little surreal about watching someone grow up. There are the obvious changes from old photos and questionable childhood haircuts, but what confuses me is the subtle, quieter change. One day you realize the person you've known for as long as you can remember is becoming someone you're still getting to know. I've known Saira for so long that I can't say when our friendship started. We met at our local mosque, which for much of our childhoods felt like an extension of our social lives. Endless Ramadan programs, weekend gatherings and lazy afternoons at each other's houses made it impossible to not form a strong bond from the start. We made friendship bracelets at youth events, tied with varying levels of skill depending on our age, and talked about random things that took up our whole afternoon. We never made plans weeks ahead. We didn't need to. If I couldn't get a ride to her house, I knew I'd see her within a few days at the next community event. At that age, you don't think about how friendships work, if you're getting closer or drifting apart, if you're both putting in the same effort or if you'll still be talking in ten years. Saira was just there. And when you're a kid, it's easy to assume that whatever is always around will never change. Things look pretty different now. I'm a sophomore in college in Baltimore, and she's finishing her senior year of high school back in New Jersey. Our friendship lives in text messages, quick Snapchat photos and short visits squeezed into academic breaks. We don't talk every day, but when we do, we send each other small pieces of our days. That could be something funny that happened on the walk to class, or a photo with no context that would confuse anyone else but makes perfect sense to us. It's a different kind of closeness than what we had growing up. Back then we shared things because we happened to be in the same room, but things are different when proximity no longer exists to force conversation. Lately I've been helping her with her college applications, which is a funny spot to be in. Not long ago I was the one spiraling over my personal statement and venting to her about deadlines. Now I'm the one giving advice and trying to convince her everything will turn out fine. I know that doesn't feel very reassuring when you're in the middle of it, but I say it anyway, because it's true. Soon she'll be on a campus of her own, building new routines and meeting new people. She'll find out what it's like to have a dozen things due and an hour to get them done. I'm genuinely excited for her. I also can't quite believe we're at this stage already. When did the kids making string bracelets turn into people stressing over admissions? When did growing up stop being something far off and become the everyday business of checking whether we're both free on a certain weekend? I don't have an answer. I think it happened so gradually that neither of us noticed. What comforts me is that the friendship has changed without losing what it was. We don't need to talk every day to stay part of each other's lives, and we don't need to recreate our childhood to value the history we have. One text can pick up right where we left off, because the familiarity is still there. Maybe that's what I treasure most about a childhood friend. Saira knew me before I had any real idea who I wanted to be. She knew me before the pressure of our futures, and before life got so busy that keeping up with people started to feel like an item on a to-do list. I used to think a good friendship meant nothing about it would change. Now I think it's the opposite. The friendships that last are the ones that make room for who each person is becoming, even as life takes you in different directions. Aliyah Merchant is a sophomore from Hillsborough, N.J. majoring in Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering.

articles.title: Why are we wired toward wired headphones?
articles.description: Look, I remember the 2018 era when AirPods were the status symbol. Middle school hallways were filled with awkward children all playing the part of being cool because we had wireless headphones. The emphasis was on the less: less cord, less tangle, less evidence that we were attached to anything at all. The goal was effortlessness, demonstrated through two white stems sitting in our ears, like we were born with them. We were untouchable. Here I am, eight years later, walking to class with the white cord swinging around my jacket. I am not alone. Look around Brody, the Beach or even the BSC; you'll see them everywhere, dangling from sweatshirt collars and plugged into laptops. It's official: the cord is back. The practical argument is tempting as it is truthful. It's easy: wired headphones don't need charging nor announce mid-lecture recording that your battery is at 10%. They don't connect to your roommate's laptop randomly, nor do they refuse to pair to your phone. I have never lost exactly one of them. They cost the same price as a meal at an overpriced cafe, so when mine inevitably frayed after 2 years of use, I didn't particularly mourn my wallet. I don't think practicality explains all of the wire. I think we missed the wire itself. A wire is honest in that it tells everyone around you that you are listening to something, a clearer signal than an AirPod tucked away into an ear. It is the delicate yet firm "not right now", yet it also runs the other direction: when you hand someone an earbud, you can only drift three feet apart. I calculated that distance on an Amtrak to DC with my best friends as we leaned together so the cord wouldn't pull. Wireless earbuds can be shared too, but nothing holds you there or tethers you to something warm and real. Walk away, and the song just follows you. Part of me wants to point out that we are all, literally, wired: every sound we've ever heard is a stutter of signals running down a physical line, neurons passing a tone, a note, a song throughout our brains. Is that why the cord feels trustworthy? I can trace it, from my phone to my ears. Nothing floats through the air on faith. The tangles hold their own charm. Pulling a knot of cord from my pocket and working it loose is thirty seconds in which my hands are busy and my phone is not: it is an act of devotion. The wireless years have promised freedom and delivered. Everything lives in the cloud, updates overnight and drifts, far from our grasp. But this freedom from everything feels more like floating, so we reach back for the one thing that stays put. In 2018, the emphasis was on the less. It turns out I never wanted less. I wanted something to hold onto. Thansi Garikipati is a sophomore majoring in Biophysics and Writing Seminars from Edmond, Okla. She is the Public Editor of The News-Letter.

articles.title: Embracing physical media in the modern age
articles.description: I was snooping around my dad's house when I found a sizeable, sturdy black bag on a bookshelf in his office. I was 13, dressed in his Soundgarden T-shirt and a pair of out-of-date cargo jeans. I unzipped the bag and beheld a new world - or an old world, I suppose. Hundreds of CDs were lying in buckling plastic sleeves, ripe for the taking: pirated Alice in Chains live concerts, Deftones' Saturday Night Wrist, Sepultura's Roots, Primus' Sailing the Seas of Cheese and… Fiona Apple's Tidal? I dragged the bag into my room, carefully removing all of our shared favorites before flipping back through to retrieve music unheard by me before, selecting solely based on the quality of the cover images. I had a feeling I wouldn't like Monster Magnet, but the Superjudge art was too good to resist. Eventually, I stumbled upon what was the greatest album ever made to 13-year-old me: David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars. But how could I jump back in time without a machine? The holidays were rapidly approaching, and I had many wishes, but none as great as getting a CD player. Not portable - I refused to risk scratching my precious new hand-me-downs - but dormant. I didn't want another opportunity to live with my headphones in, ignoring my AP Human Geography teacher and missing instructions to get on stage at my music school. No - I wanted to sit down and listen and not do anything else for a while. I didn't want to listen and play Tetris, or listen and scroll on Instagram, or listen and text my friends. I wanted to be on my own, in a way I imagined people used to be. I wanted to feel how my dad and everyone must have felt, before music was wedged between a calculator and a compass on a digital screen. Upon hearing of my new affinity for physical music, my family members opened their varied, extensive collections to my very sticky fingers. Suddenly I had three versions of Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon, two of Fleetwood Mac's Rumors, two of Nick Drake's Pink Moon and a partridge in a pear tree. Despite their generosity, they all asked me a question that I found baffling: why would you want these old things when you can stream anything you want? For a long time, I couldn't answer this seemingly simple question. Maybe I was endeared by the past, holding nostalgia for a time I never experienced. Maybe it made me feel unique, as many pre-teens long to feel. Or maybe I liked focusing on the music instead of letting it play idly in the background; forcing myself to listen to full discographies to give myself a music education; and how access to limited options encouraged me to do both of those things. Christmas mixes from the mid-2000s, every Jimi Hendrix album, Outkast, Black Sabbath and Led Zeppelin rang through my room. Names I had never heard before, from Townes Van Zandt to Dio, began to make music to me. Of course, a lot of what I listened to I would never play again even if met with the punishment of certain death, but I always insisted on listening all the way through the albums before I made a judgement. It was a way to reject the millions of ways to mix, shuffle and parse albums into playlists that I was used to. For years, I scoured thrift stores and begged on birthdays, all in an attempt to expand my collection, refine it to my own taste, make it my own. I slowly succeeded, filling out CD cases with my own finds. When I began to drive in 2023, my 2013 Honda CRV, Sally, was miraculously equipped with a CD player. I drove to school and back, unplugged, almost always. On foggy New England mornings in autumn and spring, I let Bon Iver's For Emma and Sufjan Stevens' Carrie and Lowell soften my drive to school. When I shivered in the car in January, starting to drive before my windshield defrosted (a tendency that eventually cost Sally some of her faculties), Radiohead's Kid A and Songs of Leonard Cohen accompanied me on my way. In the breezy summer, with the windows down and my best friend in the passenger seat, too nervous to drive us herself, it was Adrianne Lenker's songs or The Best of the Eagles, volumes one and two playing back to back while we sang along. The electricity of those moments felt different, calmer, than what I was used to. Even the soft buzzing sound of the CD turning gave me comfort, knowing something tangible and physical was making the chords ring out, preserving my sense of being tethered to the real world. Now, Sally the Honda CRV is gone, and my dad is far away. The broken piece of plastic that's supposed to form the front half of the CD case for David Bowie's Diamond Dogs clatters to the floor; I elbowed it off my desk trying to finish my makeup before my formal. Still, my simple black CD player from six years ago dutifully reproduces the twanging, smooth peaks and drifts of "Sweet Thing." I'm excited to go out and watch the DJ pretend to twist knobs while playing a Spotify blend through a lousy JBL speaker, dancing along with my friends and sisters. But I love these moments just as much, experiencing music away from the phone I'll use tonight to coordinate timing with others, take pictures, call an Uber, pay and post those pictures. I love being able to put my phone away without losing music with it. Julia Schager is a junior majoring in International Studies and History from Stamford, Conn. She is a Copy Editor for The News-Letter.
